final_answer: Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, a process where bacteria with genetic mutations conferring resistance to antibiotics survive and proliferate. When antibiotics are used, they kill susceptible bacteria, but resistant strains, which may have acquired resistance genes via mutation or horizontal gene transfer, survive. Over time, these resistant bacteria become dominant. Overprescription accelerates this by increasing selective pressure: excessive or inappropriate antibiotic use exposes more bacteria to drugs, allowing resistant variants to thrive. Incomplete treatment courses or broad-spectrum antibiotics further reduce competition, enabling resistant strains to spread. This creates an environment where resistance evolves faster than new drugs can be developed.
